summary.text: The defining sum yields the recurrence \(a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\); for odd \(p\), Fermat’s theorem and the binomial identity for \(\binom{q+2(p-1)}2\) make its coefficient and forcing term invariant under the shift \(2(p-1)\), with the vanishing coefficient at the aligned initial step supplying the base case for induction. For \(p=2\), the recurrence shows that all consecutive terms from index \(1\) onward are equal modulo \(2\), hence in particular invariant under the required shift.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),
\]
where an empty product is understood to be \(1\). Since
\(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\), this is exactly the sequence in the statement.
We prove that for every prime \(p\), every \(n\geq 1\), and
\[
 T=2(p-1),
\]
one has
\[
 a(n+T)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

First we derive a recurrence for \(a(n)\). In the sum defining \(a(n+1)\), the term with \(k=n\) is
\[
 2^{\binom{n+1}{2}},
\]
because its product is empty. For each of the other terms, where \(0\leq k<n\), the product acquires one new final factor, namely \(2^n-1\):
\[
 \prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(2^j-1)
 =(2^n-1)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \boxed{a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}.}\tag{1}
\]
This identity holds for every \(n\geq 0\).

We will also use the elementary identity
\[
 \binom{q+t}{2}=\binom q2+tq+\binom t2.\tag{2}
\]
It follows either by expanding \(r(r-1)/2\), or by induction on \(t\).

We first handle an odd prime \(p\). All equations in the next part are taken modulo \(p\). Since \(p\neq 2\), the residue of \(2\) is nonzero, and Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
 2^{p-1}=1.\tag{3}
\]
In particular, for \(T=2(p-1)\),
\[
 2^T=(2^{p-1})^2=1.\tag{4}
\]
It follows at once that for every \(r\geq 0\),
\[
 2^{r+T}=2^r2^T=2^r.\tag{5}
\]
Thus the coefficient \(2^r-1\) in recurrence (1) is unchanged when \(r\) is replaced by \(r+T\).

We next show that the inhomogeneous power of \(2\) in (1) is also unchanged by this shift. We claim that for every \(q\geq 0\),
\[
 2^{\binom{q+T}{2}}=2^{\binom q2}\pmod p.\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, by (2),
\[
 \binom{q+T}{2}=\binom q2+Tq+\binom T2.
\]
The middle summand is
\[
 Tq=2(p-1)q,
\]
which is divisible by \(p-1\). Moreover,
\[
 \binom T2=\frac{T(T-1)}2
 =\frac{2(p-1)(2(p-1)-1)}2
 =(p-1)(2(p-1)-1),
\]
so this summand is also divisible by \(p-1\). Hence the difference
\(\binom{q+T}{2}-\binom q2\) is divisible by \(p-1\). Equation (3) therefore proves (6). Equivalently, taking \(q=r+1\),
\[
 2^{\binom{r+T+1}{2}}=2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}\pmod p.\tag{7}
\]

For clarity, write \(A_r\) for the residue class of \(a(r)\) modulo \(p\). Reducing (1) modulo \(p\), we have
\[
 A_{r+1}=(2^r-1)A_r+2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}.\tag{8}
\]
We prove by induction on \(m\geq 0\) that
\[
 A_{m+1+T}=A_{m+1}.\tag{9}
\]

For the base case \(m=0\), apply (8) at \(r=T\). By (4), the coefficient \(2^T-1\) is zero, so
\[
 A_{T+1}=2^{\binom{T+1}{2}}.
\]
On the other hand, applying (8) at \(r=0\), the coefficient \(2^0-1\) is also zero, and hence
\[
 A_1=2^{\binom12}.
\]
Equation (6), with \(q=1\), says that the two powers on the right are equal. Thus \(A_{T+1}=A_1\), proving the base case.

Now suppose that
\[
 A_{m+1+T}=A_{m+1}.
\]
Put \(r=m+1\). We must prove \(A_{r+1+T}=A_{r+1}\). There are two possible cases, which also explain the “reset” mechanism in the recurrence.

If \(2^r=1\pmod p\), then by (5) also \(2^{r+T}=1\pmod p\). Thus the coefficient of the preceding sequence value vanishes in both instances of (8). Therefore
\[
 A_{r+1}=2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 A_{r+T+1}=2^{\binom{r+T+1}{2}}.
\]
These are equal by (7). In this case the desired equality is forced independently of the induction hypothesis.

If \(2^r\neq 1\pmod p\), apply (8) at \(r\) and at \(r+T\):
\[
 A_{r+1}=(2^r-1)A_r+2^{\binom{r+1}{2}},
\]
while
\[
 A_{r+T+1}=(2^{r+T}-1)A_{r+T}
             +2^{\binom{r+T+1}{2}}.
\]
By (5), the two coefficients are equal; by the induction hypothesis,
\(A_{r+T}=A_r\); and by (7), the two final powers are equal. Thus the two right-hand sides agree, proving
\(A_{r+T+1}=A_{r+1}\). (In fact, this argument also works in the reset case, but the split makes explicit why alignment begins at index \(1\).)

This completes the induction. Hence for every odd prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\), writing \(n=m+1\), we obtain
\[
 a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p.\tag{10}
\]

It remains to consider the prime \(p=2\). Reduce recurrence (1) modulo \(2\). Let \(r\geq 1\). Then \(2^r=0\pmod 2\), so
\[
 2^r-1=-1=1\pmod 2.
\]
Also \(\binom{r+1}{2}>0\), because \(r\geq 1\). Therefore
\[
 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}=0\pmod 2.
\]
Recurrence (1) now becomes simply
\[
 a(r+1)\equiv a(r)\pmod 2\qquad(r\geq 1).\tag{11}
\]
Thus all terms beginning with \(a(1)\) have the same residue modulo \(2\). In particular, for every \(n\geq 1\), applying (11) twice gives
\[
 a(n+2)\equiv a(n+1)\equiv a(n)\pmod 2.
\]
Since \(2(p-1)=2\) when \(p=2\), this is exactly the required assertion in the remaining case.

Combining the odd-prime case with the case \(p=2\), we conclude that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
 \boxed{a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p.}
\]
